session.goal: Write a technical RFC for migrating from monolith to microservices with iterative feedback and revisions

content_blocks.text: You are a senior distributed systems architect. Help the user write a production-quality RFC for migrating a monolithic application to a microservices architecture. Be thorough, cite industry patterns, and respond to feedback iteratively. Structure the RFC with standard sections: motivation, goals, non-goals, design, migration strategy, risks, and rollback plan.

I need to write an RFC for migrating our e-commerce platform from a Django monolith to microservices. The monolith handles catalog, orders, payments, user accounts, notifications, and inventory. We have about 200 engineers across 8 teams, 40M monthly active users, and the deploy pipeline takes 45 minutes end-to-end with frequent rollback due to coupling. Can you draft the initial RFC structure and the motivation section?

# RFC-2026-037: Monolith-to-Microservices Migration — E-Commerce Platform

## Status: Draft
## Authors: [Platform Architecture Team]
## Date: 2026-03-31

---

## 1. Motivation

Our e-commerce platform currently runs as a single Django monolith serving all six core domains: catalog, orders, payments, user accounts, notifications, and inventory. While this architecture served us well during early growth, we have reached inflection points across multiple operational dimensions that necessitate decomposition.

### 1.1 Deploy Velocity Bottleneck
The current end-to-end deploy pipeline takes 45 minutes. With 200 engineers across 8 teams committing to a shared trunk, the deploy queue creates a 3-5 hour feedback loop from merge to production. Coupled modules mean that a change to the notification template rendering engine requires a full regression suite covering payments and inventory — domains with zero functional overlap.

### 1.2 Blast Radius of Failures
In Q4 2025, a memory leak in the catalog search indexer caused OOM kills that took down the entire platform, including payments processing. Post-incident analysis showed that 73% of our P1 incidents in the past 12 months had blast radii extending beyond the originating domain due to shared process boundaries.

### 1.3 Scaling Asymmetry
Catalog read traffic follows diurnal patterns with 10x peaks during flash sales, while payment processing is relatively steady. The monolith forces uniform scaling: we provision for peak catalog load, resulting in 4x over-provisioning of payment processing capacity, costing approximately $2.1M/year in excess compute.

### 1.4 Team Autonomy
Domain boundaries in the codebase do not enforce isolation. Teams routinely reach across module boundaries through direct database queries, shared ORM models, and in-process function calls. This creates implicit coupling that surfaces as merge conflicts (avg 12/week cross-team), broken contracts, and coordination overhead estimated at 15-20% of engineering time.

### 1.5 Technology Lock-in
All domains are constrained to Django 4.2/Python 3.11/PostgreSQL 15. The ML team needs to deploy real-time recommendation models that require GPU inference and would benefit from a Go or Rust serving layer. The notifications team wants to adopt an event-driven architecture with Kafka, but the synchronous request-response pattern of the monolith makes this impractical without architectural changes.

---

## 2. Goals
- Independent deployability per domain service (target: <10 min deploy per service)
- Fault isolation: failures in one domain do not cascade to others
- Independent scaling per domain based on actual traffic patterns
- Team autonomy: each team owns their service, schema, and deploy pipeline
- Incremental migration: no big-bang cutover; strangler fig pattern

## 3. Non-Goals
- Rewriting business logic (lift-and-shift, then optimize)
- Migrating to a different cloud provider
- Adopting Kubernetes (already on K8s)
- Changing the customer-facing API contract

## 4. Design (to be expanded)
## 5. Migration Strategy (to be expanded)
## 6. Risks & Mitigations (to be expanded)
## 7. Rollback Plan (to be expanded)
## 8. Open Questions (to be expanded)

---

Shall I proceed with the Design section next, or would you like to revise the motivation and goals first?

Good start. Two revisions on the motivation: (1) in section 1.2, the actual incident was a catalog Elasticsearch reindexing job that saturated the shared PostgreSQL connection pool, not a memory leak — fix that. (2) Add a section 1.6 about compliance: our payments domain needs PCI-DSS scope reduction and the monolith makes the entire codebase in-scope for PCI audits. Then proceed to the Design section — I want to see the proposed service boundaries, communication patterns, and data ownership model.

### 1.2 Blast Radius of Failures (revised)
In Q4 2025, a catalog Elasticsearch reindexing job saturated the shared PostgreSQL connection pool, starving the payments and order-processing paths of database connections and causing platform-wide request failures for 47 minutes. Post-incident analysis showed that 73% of our P1 incidents in the past 12 months had blast radii extending beyond the originating domain due to shared infrastructure resources — connection pools, thread pools, and memory arenas — within the monolith process.

### 1.6 Compliance Scope Reduction
Our payments domain is subject to PCI-DSS Level 1 compliance. In the monolithic architecture, the entire codebase, infrastructure, and CI/CD pipeline falls within PCI audit scope because the payments code shares a runtime, database, and deploy artifact with all other domains. Extracting payments into an isolated service with its own database, network segment, and deploy pipeline would reduce PCI scope from ~850K LOC to ~45K LOC, cutting audit preparation time by an estimated 60% and reducing the risk of audit findings in unrelated domains triggering compliance remediation.

---

## 4. Design

### 4.1 Proposed Service Boundaries

We propose six bounded contexts, each becoming an independently deployable service:

| Service | Domain | Owner Team | Primary Data Store | Estimated RPS (p50/p99) |
|---------|--------|-----------|-------------------|------------------------|
| `catalog-service` | Product listings, search, categories, pricing | Catalog Team | PostgreSQL + Elasticsearch | 12,000 / 45,000 |
| `order-service` | Order lifecycle, cart, checkout orchestration | Orders Team | PostgreSQL | 800 / 3,200 |
| `payment-service` | Payment processing, refunds, ledger | Payments Team | PostgreSQL (PCI-isolated) | 400 / 1,600 |
| `account-service` | User profiles, authentication, preferences | Identity Team | PostgreSQL + Redis | 2,000 / 8,000 |
| `notification-service` | Email, SMS, push, in-app notifications | Comms Team | PostgreSQL + Kafka | 1,500 / 6,000 |
| `inventory-service` | Stock levels, reservations, warehouse sync | Supply Chain Team | PostgreSQL + Redis | 600 / 2,400 |

### 4.2 Communication Patterns

**Synchronous (gRPC):** Used for request-path calls where the caller needs an immediate response. Examples:
- `order-service` → `payment-service`: Process payment during checkout
- `order-service` → `inventory-service`: Reserve stock during checkout
- `catalog-service` → `inventory-service`: Check availability for product pages

**Asynchronous (Kafka events):** Used for eventual consistency and domain event propagation. Examples:
- `order-service` publishes `OrderCompleted` → consumed by `notification-service`, `inventory-service`
- `payment-service` publishes `PaymentCaptured` → consumed by `order-service`, `account-service`
- `inventory-service` publishes `StockDepleted` → consumed by `catalog-service` (marks items unavailable)

**Event Schema Registry:** All events use Avro schemas registered in Confluent Schema Registry with backward-compatible evolution rules. Breaking changes require a new topic version (e.g., `orders.v2.completed`).

### 4.3 Data Ownership Model

**Principle: Each service owns its data exclusively.** No service reads or writes another service's database directly.

- **catalog-service** owns `products`, `categories`, `pricing_rules` tables → migrated to dedicated PostgreSQL instance + Elasticsearch cluster
- **order-service** owns `orders`, `order_items`, `carts` → dedicated PostgreSQL instance
- **payment-service** owns `transactions`, `refunds`, `payment_methods`, `ledger_entries` → PCI-isolated PostgreSQL in a separate VPC
- **account-service** owns `users`, `sessions`, `preferences` → dedicated PostgreSQL + Redis for session cache
- **notification-service** owns `notification_templates`, `delivery_log` → dedicated PostgreSQL + Kafka consumer group state
- **inventory-service** owns `stock_levels`, `reservations`, `warehouse_locations` → dedicated PostgreSQL + Redis for real-time stock cache

**Cross-service data access** is handled through:
1. **API calls** for real-time reads (e.g., order-service calls account-service to resolve user display name)
2. **Event-driven materialized views** for read-heavy cross-domain queries (e.g., catalog-service maintains a denormalized stock availability view from inventory events)
3. **CQRS read models** where needed for complex aggregations (e.g., admin dashboard aggregating across services)

### 4.4 API Gateway & Service Mesh

- **API Gateway (Kong):** Routes external traffic, handles rate limiting, authentication token validation, and request transformation. The customer-facing REST API contract remains unchanged — the gateway maps existing endpoints to the appropriate backend service.
- **Service Mesh (Istio):** Manages inter-service communication with mTLS, circuit breaking, retry policies, and observability. Each service gets an Envoy sidecar.
- **Service Discovery:** Kubernetes-native DNS (service.namespace.svc.cluster.local) with Istio's control plane managing the service registry.

Shall I continue with the Migration Strategy section, or do you want to revise the service boundaries or communication patterns?

The design looks solid. One concern: you mentioned gRPC for synchronous calls, but our frontend is a Next.js app that currently calls REST endpoints. I don't want to introduce a protocol translation layer at the gateway for external traffic. Can you clarify: is gRPC only for internal service-to-service, with REST preserved for the external API? Also, for the data ownership model in section 4.3, what happens to the existing shared PostgreSQL during migration? We can't do a big-bang database split. Address these in the design, then move to Migration Strategy.

Great clarifications. Let me address both points directly and then proceed to Migration Strategy.

### 4.2 Communication Patterns (revised addendum)

**External (REST/JSON over HTTPS):** The customer-facing API remains REST. The Next.js frontend continues calling the same REST endpoints through the Kong API Gateway. No protocol translation is needed — the gateway routes REST requests to the appropriate service, and each service exposes a REST API for external consumption.

**Internal (gRPC with Protocol Buffers):** Service-to-service calls use gRPC for performance (binary serialization, HTTP/2 multiplexing, streaming support) and contract enforcement (proto files as the source of truth). This is strictly internal — no gRPC is exposed through the API gateway.

**Summary:**
```
Next.js Frontend → REST/JSON → Kong Gateway → REST/JSON → Target Service
Service A → gRPC → Service B  (internal only, via Istio mesh)
Service X → Kafka Event → Service Y  (async, internal only)
```

### 4.3 Data Ownership Model (revised addendum — Database Migration Path)

**The shared PostgreSQL is split incrementally using the Database-per-Service pattern with a transitional dual-write/dual-read phase:**

**Phase 1 — Schema Isolation (weeks 1-4):** Within the existing shared PostgreSQL instance, enforce schema-level isolation. Each service gets its own PostgreSQL schema (e.g., `catalog.*`, `orders.*`). Cross-schema foreign keys are identified and replaced with application-level references. This is a logical split, not a physical one.

**Phase 2 — Read Path Migration (weeks 5-12):** Each service begins reading from its own schema exclusively. Cross-domain reads that previously used JOINs across schemas are replaced with API calls or event-driven materialized views. The Change Data Capture (CDC) pipeline (Debezium) streams changes from the shared database to service-specific materialized views during transition.

**Phase 3 — Write Path Migration (weeks 13-20):** Each service becomes the sole writer to its schema. Any remaining writes from other services are routed through the owning service's API. Debezium CDC validates that no rogue writes occur.

**Phase 4 — Physical Split (weeks 21-28):** Each schema is promoted to its own PostgreSQL instance using logical replication. The shared database becomes a read-only fallback for 2 weeks, then is decommissioned. Payment-service gets its own RDS instance in a PCI-isolated VPC from Phase 2 onward (accelerated timeline due to compliance requirements).

---

## 5. Migration Strategy

### 5.1 Approach: Strangler Fig Pattern

We adopt the Strangler Fig pattern: new services are deployed alongside the monolith, and traffic is incrementally shifted from monolith endpoints to service endpoints via the API gateway. The monolith shrinks over time as domains are extracted.

### 5.2 Extraction Order

Services are extracted in order of decreasing independence and business value:

| Phase | Service | Rationale | Duration | Risk |
|-------|---------|-----------|----------|------|
| 1 | `notification-service` | Fewest inbound dependencies, event-driven natural fit, low blast radius if extraction fails | 6 weeks | Low |
| 2 | `account-service` | Well-defined API surface (auth/profile), depended on by others but with a stable contract | 8 weeks | Medium |
| 3 | `catalog-service` | Highest traffic, already has Elasticsearch as a semi-independent data store, benefits most from independent scaling | 10 weeks | Medium |
| 4 | `inventory-service` | Tightly coupled to catalog and orders; extract after catalog to avoid circular dependencies during transition | 8 weeks | Medium |
| 5 | `payment-service` | PCI compliance driver, but complex transactional boundaries with order-service; needs order-service integration points stable first | 10 weeks | High |
| 6 | `order-service` | Extracted last because it orchestrates checkout across payments, inventory, and notifications; all dependencies must be stable | 12 weeks | High |

### 5.3 Traffic Shifting Strategy

For each service extraction:
1. **Dark launch (week 1-2):** Service deployed, receives shadowed traffic (duplicate of production requests), responses compared but not served to users.
2. **Canary (week 3-4):** 5% → 25% → 50% traffic shift via Kong weighted routing. Automated rollback if error rate exceeds 0.1% delta from monolith baseline or p99 latency increases >15%.
3. **Full cutover (week 5-6):** 100% traffic to new service. Monolith endpoint deprecated but kept as fallback for 2 weeks.
4. **Monolith code removal (week 7+):** Dead code in monolith is removed, database tables ownership transferred.

### 5.4 Shared Libraries and Cross-Cutting Concerns

During migration, the following are extracted as shared libraries (published to internal PyPI/npm):
- **Authentication middleware:** JWT validation, session resolution
- **Observability SDK:** Structured logging, distributed tracing (OpenTelemetry), metrics emission
- **Event contracts:** Avro schema definitions, Kafka producer/consumer wrappers
- **Error taxonomy:** Standardized error codes and response formats

These libraries are versioned independently and follow semantic versioning to avoid recreating the coupling problem at the library level.

Ready for Risks & Mitigations next?

Yes, proceed with Risks & Mitigations. I want you to be thorough here — cover distributed systems risks (network partitions, data consistency, observability gaps), organizational risks (team readiness, Conway's Law misalignment), and migration-specific risks (data loss during DB split, traffic shifting failures). For each risk, give severity, likelihood, and a concrete mitigation — not just 'monitor it'.

## 6. Risks & Mitigations

### 6.1 Distributed Systems Risks

**R1: Data Consistency Across Service Boundaries**
- **Severity:** Critical | **Likelihood:** High
- **Description:** The monolith currently relies on ACID transactions spanning catalog, orders, inventory, and payments (e.g., checkout: reserve stock + create order + initiate payment in one transaction). Decomposition breaks these into cross-service operations where partial failures leave the system in an inconsistent state.
- **Mitigation:** Implement the Saga pattern for multi-service transactions. The checkout flow becomes an orchestrated saga managed by `order-service`:
  1. `inventory-service.ReserveStock()` — compensating: `ReleaseStock()`
  2. `payment-service.AuthorizePayment()` — compensating: `VoidAuthorization()`
  3. `order-service.ConfirmOrder()` — compensating: `CancelOrder()`
  Each step has an explicit compensating action. Saga state is persisted in `order-service`'s database with a state machine (states: INITIATED → STOCK_RESERVED → PAYMENT_AUTHORIZED → CONFIRMED | COMPENSATING → FAILED). Temporal.io is the saga orchestrator to avoid hand-rolling retry/timeout/compensation logic.

**R2: Network Partition Between Services**
- **Severity:** High | **Likelihood:** Medium
- **Description:** Inter-service gRPC calls introduce network failure modes that don't exist in the monolith. A network partition between `order-service` and `payment-service` during checkout could leave orders in a limbo state.
- **Mitigation:** 
  - Circuit breakers (Istio + application-level via `resilience4j`) with fallback behavior: if `payment-service` is unreachable, `order-service` queues the payment request to a Kafka dead-letter topic and returns "order pending payment confirmation" to the user.
  - Retry budgets: max 3 retries with exponential backoff (100ms, 400ms, 1600ms) + jitter. Total timeout budget per user request: 5 seconds.
  - Idempotency keys on all mutating operations to prevent duplicate processing on retries.

**R3: Observability Gaps in Distributed Tracing**
- **Severity:** High | **Likelihood:** High
- **Description:** In the monolith, a single request produces a single log trail. In microservices, a checkout request fans out across 4 services, and correlating logs/traces across service boundaries is non-trivial. Teams will struggle to debug cross-service issues without proper tooling.
- **Mitigation:**
  - Mandatory OpenTelemetry SDK integration in every service (enforced via CI lint rule that fails builds without trace context propagation).
  - W3C Trace Context headers propagated through all gRPC and REST calls.
  - Centralized tracing backend (Jaeger) with service dependency map.
  - Structured logging with mandatory fields: `trace_id`, `span_id`, `service_name`, `request_id`. Log aggregation in Elasticsearch with Kibana dashboards per service and cross-service views.
  - Runbook: Every service must ship with a troubleshooting runbook that maps common error patterns to root causes. Required for production readiness review.

**R4: Cascading Failure via Shared Infrastructure**
- **Severity:** Critical | **Likelihood:** Medium
- **Description:** Even with service isolation, shared infrastructure (Kafka cluster, Kubernetes control plane, DNS, API gateway) remains a single point of failure. A Kafka broker failure could disrupt event-driven communication across all services simultaneously.
- **Mitigation:**
  - Kafka: Multi-AZ deployment, replication factor 3, min.insync.replicas=2. Consumer services must handle Kafka unavailability gracefully (local queue + retry).
  - Kong Gateway: Active-active deployment across 3 AZs with health-check-based failover.
  - Each service must pass a "dependency isolation test": it must degrade gracefully (not crash) when any downstream dependency is unavailable for 60 seconds.

### 6.2 Organizational Risks

**R5: Conway's Law Misalignment**
- **Severity:** High | **Likelihood:** Medium
- **Description:** Our current team structure doesn't perfectly map to the proposed service boundaries. The "Platform" team currently owns both inventory and catalog code. The "Checkout" team owns both orders and payments. If we decompose services without reorganizing teams, we'll end up with shared ownership that recreates the coupling at the organizational level.
- **Mitigation:**
  - Reorganize teams before or concurrent with service extraction. Proposed mapping is in section 4.1. Each service has exactly one owning team. The Platform team splits into Catalog Team and Supply Chain Team. The Checkout team splits into Orders Team and Payments Team.
  - Transition period: For 8 weeks after reorg, engineers from the original combined team are embedded in both new teams to transfer knowledge. After 8 weeks, clean ownership boundary enforced.

**R6: Insufficient Distributed Systems Expertise**
- **Severity:** Medium | **Likelihood:** High
- **Description:** Most of our 200 engineers have only worked with the Django monolith. Distributed systems patterns (saga, eventual consistency, idempotency, circuit breaking) are unfamiliar territory. Mistakes in these areas cause production incidents.
- **Mitigation:**
  - 2-week distributed systems bootcamp before Phase 1 begins. Covers: CAP theorem in practice, saga pattern, idempotency, circuit breakers, distributed tracing.
  - Embed one distributed systems senior engineer (internal or contracted) per team for the first two extraction phases.
  - Shared libraries (section 5.4) encapsulate the hardest patterns so individual teams don't implement them from scratch.
  - Chaos engineering game days: monthly Litmus chaos experiments targeting network latency injection, pod kills, and Kafka partition leader elections.

### 6.3 Migration-Specific Risks

**R7: Data Loss or Corruption During Database Split**
- **Severity:** Critical | **Likelihood:** Medium
- **Description:** The Phase 3→4 database split (section 4.3) involves logical replication from the shared PostgreSQL to service-specific instances. Replication lag, schema drift, or missed sequences could cause data loss or inconsistency.
- **Mitigation:**
  - Dual-write verification: During Phase 3, every write goes to both old and new databases. A background reconciliation job compares row counts, checksums, and latest timestamps every 5 minutes and alerts on divergence >0.
  - Before Phase 4 cutover: full table-level checksum comparison (using `pg_checksums` + application-level row hashing) between shared DB and service DB. Cutover blocked if any divergence detected.
  - Point-in-time recovery (PITR) configured on all new instances with 7-day retention. Automated backup verification (restore-to-test-instance) daily.
  - Rollback path: If data issues detected within 48 hours of cutover, revert service to read from shared DB (still available as read-only) while issues are resolved.

**R8: Traffic Shifting Regression**
- **Severity:** High | **Likelihood:** Medium
- **Description:** During canary deployment (section 5.3), subtle behavioral differences between the monolith and new service may not be caught by error rate monitoring alone. Examples: different JSON serialization of edge-case Unicode, different pagination behavior, different handling of null fields.
- **Mitigation:**
  - Shadow traffic comparison during dark launch phase: 100% of production requests are duplicated to the new service, and responses are compared field-by-field. Differences logged and categorized. Must reach <0.01% semantic difference rate before entering canary phase.
  - Integration test suite that runs against both monolith and new service endpoints with identical inputs, comparing outputs. This suite is the gate for canary promotion.
  - Feature flags (LaunchDarkly) for gradual rollout at the business logic level, independent of traffic shifting. Allows reverting specific behaviors without reverting all traffic.

**R9: Increased Latency from Network Hops**
- **Severity:** Medium | **Likelihood:** High
- **Description:** Operations that were in-process function calls (sub-millisecond) become network calls (1-10ms per hop). A checkout flow that touches 4 services could add 20-40ms of latency, impacting conversion rates.
- **Mitigation:**
  - Latency budget per user-facing endpoint. Checkout target: <300ms p99 (current monolith: ~180ms p99). Budget allocated: 80ms gateway + 120ms order-service + 50ms inventory + 50ms payment.
  - Parallel fan-out where dependencies allow: stock reservation and payment authorization can run concurrently.
  - gRPC connection pooling and keep-alive to eliminate connection setup overhead.
  - Response caching: catalog-service caches product data in Redis (TTL 60s) to avoid repeated DB queries for the same product during a user's session.
  - If p99 exceeds budget during canary: stop traffic shift, profile, optimize before resuming.

Shall I proceed with the Rollback Plan and Open Questions?

This is excellent. Before we move on — going back to R1 in section 6.1, you mentioned Temporal.io for saga orchestration. We've had reliability issues with Temporal in our staging environment (worker starvation under load). Can you propose an alternative saga implementation that doesn't depend on a third-party orchestrator? I'd prefer something we control entirely.

Good call — if Temporal's worker model has been unreliable in staging, it's a liability for the most critical path in the system. Here's a self-hosted alternative:

### R1 Mitigation (revised): Application-Level Saga with Persistent State Machine

**Replace Temporal with an application-owned saga orchestrator built into `order-service`:**

**State Machine Implementation:**
- Saga state stored in `order-service`'s PostgreSQL in a `saga_executions` table:
  ```
  saga_executions:
    saga_id (PK, UUID)
    order_id (FK)
    current_step (enum: INITIATED, STOCK_RESERVED, PAYMENT_AUTHORIZED, CONFIRMED, COMPENSATING, COMPENSATED, FAILED)
    step_attempts (JSONB: {step_name: {attempt_count, last_error, last_attempt_at}})
    created_at, updated_at, expires_at
  ```
- Each saga step is a state transition. The orchestrator reads the current state, executes the next step's gRPC call, and atomically updates the state in the same database transaction (outbox pattern for reliability).

**Execution Flow:**
1. Checkout request creates a saga record in state `INITIATED`
2. Orchestrator calls `inventory-service.ReserveStock()` → on success, transitions to `STOCK_RESERVED`
3. Orchestrator calls `payment-service.AuthorizePayment()` → on success, transitions to `PAYMENT_AUTHORIZED`
4. Orchestrator confirms order → transitions to `CONFIRMED`
5. On any step failure: transitions to `COMPENSATING`, executes compensating actions in reverse order, transitions to `COMPENSATED` or `FAILED`

**Reliability Guarantees:**
- **Crash recovery:** A background worker polls for sagas stuck in non-terminal states for >30 seconds and resumes them from their last committed step. Because state is in PostgreSQL (not in-memory), server restarts don't lose progress.
- **Idempotency:** Every step includes an idempotency key (saga_id + step_name). Downstream services deduplicate based on this key. Retrying a step that already succeeded is a no-op.
- **Timeout handling:** Each saga has an `expires_at` timestamp (default: 5 minutes from creation). Expired sagas are automatically compensated. Users see "order could not be completed, please retry."
- **Outbox pattern for events:** Instead of publishing Kafka events directly from the saga orchestrator, events are written to an `outbox` table in the same transaction as the state transition. A separate Debezium CDC connector tails the outbox table and publishes to Kafka. This guarantees exactly-once event delivery without distributed transactions.

**Why this is better than Temporal for our case:**
- Zero external dependencies beyond PostgreSQL (which we already operate and trust)
- No worker starvation risk — saga execution runs in the same process as `order-service`, scaled by our existing K8s HPA
- Full visibility: saga state is queryable via SQL, debuggable with standard tools
- Simpler operational model: no separate Temporal cluster to monitor, upgrade, and scale

**Trade-off acknowledged:** We lose Temporal's built-in workflow versioning and cron scheduling. For our use case (checkout saga with 3 steps), this is acceptable. If we need complex long-running workflows in the future, we can revisit.

Want me to continue with Rollback Plan and Open Questions now?
Perfect, the state machine approach is much better for us. Yes, go ahead with Rollback Plan and Open Questions.

## 7. Rollback Plan

### 7.1 Per-Service Rollback (During Traffic Shifting)

Each service extraction follows the traffic shifting strategy in section 5.3. Rollback is the reverse: shift traffic back to the monolith endpoint.

**Automated Rollback Triggers:**
- Error rate delta >0.1% compared to monolith baseline (measured over 5-minute sliding window)
- p99 latency increase >15% compared to monolith baseline
- Any 5xx error rate >0.5% sustained for >2 minutes
- Data consistency check failure (reconciliation job divergence >0)

**Rollback Procedure:**
1. Kong gateway weight shifted to 100% monolith within 30 seconds (pre-configured rollback route, activated via single API call or PagerDuty runbook button)
2. New service continues running but receives no production traffic
3. All in-flight requests to the new service are allowed to complete (30-second drain period)
4. Post-rollback verification: monolith health checks green for 5 minutes before declaring rollback complete
5. Incident created automatically, post-mortem required within 48 hours before re-attempting cutover

**Rollback SLA:** Full traffic revert within 2 minutes of trigger detection.

### 7.2 Database Rollback (During Physical Split)

The database migration phases (section 4.3) each have explicit rollback paths:

- **Phase 1 (Schema Isolation) rollback:** Revert schema changes via migration rollback scripts. Low risk — this is a logical reorganization within the same database.
- **Phase 2 (Read Path) rollback:** Point service read queries back to original shared tables. CDC pipeline is stopped. Materialized views dropped.
- **Phase 3 (Write Path) rollback:** Re-enable direct writes from monolith code paths. Dual-write verification ensures both databases are in sync, so rollback is safe.
- **Phase 4 (Physical Split) rollback:** The shared database is kept as read-only for 2 weeks post-cutover. If issues arise, services revert connection strings to the shared database. Data written only to the new service database during the 2-week window is replayed from the WAL (write-ahead log) to the shared database.

### 7.3 Full Migration Rollback (Emergency)

In the unlikely event that the entire migration must be abandoned after multiple services are extracted:

1. All extracted services have their traffic shifted back to monolith endpoints via Kong
2. Database connections reverted to shared PostgreSQL
3. Monolith codebase is maintained in a `monolith-fallback` branch throughout the migration — it receives security patches and critical bug fixes but no feature development
4. **Constraint:** Full rollback becomes increasingly expensive after Phase 4 (physical DB split) of the 3rd service. Beyond this point, the team must commit to forward-fixing rather than rolling back. This is the "point of no return" and should be explicitly acknowledged in the go/no-go review before Phase 4 of `catalog-service`.

---

## 8. Open Questions

| # | Question | Owner | Decision Needed By |
|---|----------|-------|--------------------|
| Q1 | Should we use a shared API gateway (Kong) or per-service gateways? Shared is simpler but creates a SPOF. Per-service adds operational overhead but improves isolation. | Platform Team | Before Phase 1 kickoff |
| Q2 | How do we handle cross-service database reporting queries that currently use JOINs across domain tables? Options: (a) CQRS read model with CDC, (b) data warehouse ETL, (c) GraphQL federation layer. | Data Team | Before Phase 2 (catalog extraction) |
| Q3 | What is the contract testing strategy? Options: (a) Pact consumer-driven contracts, (b) shared proto files with CI validation, (c) both. | QA Lead + Tech Leads | Before Phase 1 kickoff |
| Q4 | Should `notification-service` adopt Kafka Streams for event processing or use a simpler consumer-group model? Kafka Streams adds complexity but enables windowed aggregations (e.g., notification rate limiting). | Comms Team | During Phase 1 design |
| Q5 | How do we handle the monolith's Django admin interface? It currently provides CRUD access to all domain tables. Options: (a) keep it pointed at shared DB as read-only, (b) build per-service admin UIs, (c) adopt a unified admin tool (Retool/Appsmith). | Product Engineering | Before Phase 3 |
| Q6 | What is the SLO for inter-service gRPC calls? Proposed: p99 <10ms for same-AZ, <25ms for cross-AZ. Need validation from network team. | Network Team + SRE | Before Phase 1 kickoff |
| Q7 | PCI scope: Does the `order-service` need to be in PCI scope since it orchestrates payment calls, even though it doesn't handle card data directly? Legal/compliance review needed. | Compliance Team | Before Phase 5 (payment extraction) |

### 4.5 API Versioning Strategy

**Principle: version the contract, not the URL.** URL-based versioning (`/v1/`, `/v2/`) creates routing complexity and client migration burden. Instead, we use a combination of protocol-level versioning and backward-compatible evolution.

#### 4.5.1 External API (REST, customer-facing)

**Header-based versioning:**
- Clients send `Accept: application/vnd.ecommerce.v1+json`
- Default version (no header): latest stable version
- Maximum 2 supported versions at any time. Deprecation notice 6 months before removal.
- Breaking change definition: removing a field, changing a field type, changing the semantic meaning of a field, removing an endpoint. Adding new optional fields is NOT a breaking change.

**Compatibility rules:**
- **Additive changes** (new optional fields, new endpoints, new enum values): deployed without version bump. Clients must ignore unknown fields (tolerant reader pattern).
- **Breaking changes:** New version created. Kong gateway routes based on `Accept` header to the appropriate handler. Old version handler is a thin adapter that translates between old and new schemas.

#### 4.5.2 Internal API (gRPC, service-to-service)

**Protocol Buffers evolution rules:**
- Proto files are the source of truth, stored in a shared `proto/` repository with CI-enforced compatibility checks (`buf breaking` on every PR).
- **Field rules:** Never reuse field numbers. Never change field types. Deprecated fields marked with `[deprecated = true]` and reserved after removal. New fields must be optional (proto3 default).
- **Service method rules:** New methods can be added freely. Existing method signatures are immutable. If a method's semantics must change, add a new method (e.g., `CreateOrderV2`) and deprecate the old one.
- **Package versioning:** Proto packages use `v1`, `v2` namespaces only for breaking changes to method signatures: `ecommerce.orders.v1.OrderService`. Within a version, additive evolution is unlimited.
- **Rollout:** When a new proto version ships, the consuming service has 4 weeks to migrate. The producing service supports both versions during this window via a shared handler with version-specific response mapping.

#### 4.5.3 Event Schema (Kafka, async)

**Avro schemas with Confluent Schema Registry:**
- Backward compatibility mode enforced at the registry level (new schemas can read old data).
- Schema evolution: add optional fields with defaults, never remove or rename fields.
- Breaking changes: new topic (e.g., `orders.v2.completed`). Both topics published to during migration window. Consumers migrate on their own timeline within 4 weeks.

#### 4.5.4 Contract Testing

- **Pact** for REST contracts: consumer services define expected request/response pairs, provider services verify they satisfy all consumer contracts on every build.
- **buf breaking** for gRPC contracts: CI rejects PRs that make backward-incompatible proto changes.
- **Schema Registry compatibility check** for event contracts: CI rejects incompatible Avro schema changes.
- **Integration test gate:** Before any service is promoted to canary, it must pass contract tests against all current consumers.

### 4.6 Observability Stack Evaluation

The migration from monolith to microservices increases observability complexity by an order of magnitude: 6 services × 3 signal types (metrics, traces, logs) × multiple instances = hundreds of data sources. This is the right time to evaluate our observability stack, especially with the Datadog contract renewal in 6 months (September 2026).

#### Option A: Stay on Datadog

| Dimension | Assessment |
|-----------|------------|
| **Setup effort** | Low — Datadog agents already deployed, APM instrumented in Django. New services add the Datadog SDK and inherit dashboards/alerts |
| **Unified experience** | Metrics, traces, logs, and APM in one pane. Cross-service trace correlation works out of the box |
| **Cost** | Current: $380K/year for monolith. Projected with 6 services (more hosts, more custom metrics, more trace ingestion): **$550K-$650K/year** based on Datadog's per-host + per-metric pricing model. Microservices generate 5-10x more metrics and traces than monoliths |
| **Operational burden** | Low — fully managed SaaS. No infra to maintain |
| **Vendor lock-in** | High — Datadog's query language (DQL), dashboard definitions, and monitor configurations are proprietary. Migration cost increases with adoption depth |
| **Data residency** | Data stored on Datadog's infrastructure. Acceptable for most use cases but PCI logs for payment-service may require on-prem log storage |
| **Scaling** | Automatic — Datadog handles ingestion scaling |

#### Option B: Open-Source Stack (Prometheus + Grafana + Jaeger + Loki)

| Dimension | Assessment |
|-----------|------------|
| **Setup effort** | High — requires deploying and configuring 4 systems: Prometheus (metrics), Grafana (dashboards), Jaeger (traces), Loki (logs). Estimated 4-6 weeks of SRE time for production-grade setup |
| **Unified experience** | Near-parity — Grafana provides a single pane with Prometheus, Jaeger, and Loki as data sources. Cross-service correlation requires manual trace-to-log linking via trace_id (functional but less polished than Datadog) |
| **Cost** | Infrastructure: ~$80K/year for the observability cluster (compute, storage, managed Kafka for log ingestion). Engineering: 0.5 FTE SRE for ongoing maintenance. **Total: ~$120K-$150K/year** — 70-75% savings vs. projected Datadog cost |
| **Operational burden** | Medium-High — Prometheus requires capacity planning (retention, federation for multi-cluster), Loki needs index tuning, Jaeger storage backend (Elasticsearch or Cassandra) needs management |
| **Vendor lock-in** | None — all components are CNCF projects with standard APIs (PromQL, OpenTelemetry, LogQL). Dashboards and alerts are portable |
| **Data residency** | Full control — all observability data stays on our infrastructure. PCI log isolation is straightforward |
| **Scaling** | Manual — requires capacity planning. Prometheus federation or Thanos for multi-cluster. Loki scales horizontally but needs tuning |

#### Option C: Hybrid (Recommended)

**Use the open-source stack as primary, with Datadog retained for APM during the migration transition.**

**Rationale:**
1. **Cost:** $550K-$650K/year for Datadog post-migration is not justifiable when open-source alternatives provide equivalent functionality for $120K-$150K/year. The $400K+ annual savings funds 2-3 additional engineers.
2. **Migration timing:** The 6-month Datadog renewal window (September 2026) aligns with the completion of Phase 1-2 of service extraction. We can negotiate a 6-month Datadog extension (or month-to-month) rather than a full annual renewal, giving us a bridge period.
3. **OpenTelemetry as the abstraction layer:** All services instrument with OpenTelemetry SDK (already recommended in R3 mitigation). OTel collectors can export to both Datadog and Prometheus/Jaeger simultaneously during transition. This means zero re-instrumentation when we cut over.
4. **PCI compliance:** On-prem log storage for payment-service is simpler with Loki than with Datadog's log management.

**Transition Timeline:**
- **Months 1-3 (during Phase 1-2 extraction):** Deploy Prometheus + Grafana + Loki + Jaeger. OTel collectors dual-export to both Datadog and open-source stack. SRE team builds equivalent dashboards and alerts in Grafana.
- **Months 4-6:** Validate open-source stack parity with Datadog. Oncall team uses Grafana as primary, Datadog as fallback.
- **Month 6 (Datadog renewal):** If parity validated, do not renew annual contract. Negotiate 3-month extension for tail-end migration. If gaps remain, renew Datadog for 1 year and continue parallel operation.
- **Month 7-9:** Decommission Datadog agents and integrations. Full cutover to open-source stack.

**Risk mitigation:** The dual-export approach means we never lose observability data during transition. If the open-source stack proves inadequate (unlikely given maturity of CNCF projects, but possible), we simply continue with Datadog — no data loss, no blind spots.

### 5.2 Addendum: Parallelized Migration Timeline

**Parallelization analysis:**
- `notification-service` (Phase 1) and `account-service` (Phase 2) have no shared database tables or direct API dependencies. They can be extracted in parallel.
- `catalog-service` (Phase 3) and `inventory-service` (Phase 4) are coupled (catalog calls inventory for stock availability). Inventory extraction should start after catalog's read-path migration is complete (week 6 of catalog extraction), but need not wait for full catalog cutover.
- `payment-service` (Phase 5) depends on `order-service` integration points being stable, so it cannot start until order-service's API contract is frozen. However, payment-service's PCI database isolation can proceed independently.
- `order-service` (Phase 6) is extracted last because it depends on all other services being stable.

## 0. Executive Summary

This RFC proposes migrating our e-commerce platform from a Django monolith to six independently deployable microservices: catalog, orders, payments, user accounts, notifications, and inventory. The monolith currently serves 40 million monthly active users but has reached operational limits: deploy pipelines take 45 minutes with frequent rollbacks due to cross-domain coupling, a single domain failure can take down the entire platform, and uniform scaling wastes an estimated $2.1M/year in over-provisioned compute. Additionally, the monolith places our entire 850K-line codebase in PCI-DSS audit scope — a compliance burden that grows with every line of non-payment code.

The migration follows the Strangler Fig pattern: services are extracted incrementally alongside the running monolith, with traffic shifted via the API gateway using automated canary analysis and instant rollback capability. No big-bang cutover. The database is split in four phases — schema isolation, read-path migration, write-path migration, physical split — each with an explicit rollback procedure. We propose extracting services in a partially parallelized sequence over approximately 10 months, with notification-service and account-service first (lowest risk, highest independence) and order-service last (highest cross-service dependency).

The migration also presents an opportunity to reduce our observability costs. By transitioning from Datadog ($550K-$650K/year projected for microservices) to an open-source stack (Prometheus, Grafana, Jaeger, Loki at $120K-$150K/year), we project $400K+ in annual savings. A dual-export architecture using OpenTelemetry ensures zero observability gaps during the transition.

The primary risks are data consistency across service boundaries (mitigated by an application-level saga orchestrator), organizational readiness for distributed systems (mitigated by training, embedded experts, and shared libraries), and data integrity during database migration (mitigated by dual-write verification and 2-week rollback windows). The point of no return — after which rolling back to the monolith becomes impractical — is the physical database split of catalog-service, approximately 6 months into the migration, with an explicit go/no-go gate before that milestone. Across 200 engineers and 8 teams, this migration targets independent 10-minute deploys, fault isolation per domain, autonomous team ownership, and infrastructure cost reduction.
